title: Fratelli Tutti (2020)
hookLine: Francis retells the good Samaritan for a divided world
last: NOTHING AND NO ONE THROWN AWAY.

cards: Two words, Italian: fratelli tutti. All brothers. Francis of Assisi used them to address his brothers and sisters, the way someone might open a letter with dear friends.

Pope Francis took them for the title of a letter about a world split into camps: nations against nations, neighbors who won't speak, strangers left on the side of the road. He didn't open his case with a theory.
He sat down with a story Jesus told, about a man beaten and left half dead on the road to Jericho, and asked the reader a question. Which one of these people are you?

teach.h: A MAN LEFT ON THE ROAD TO JERICHO.
teach.b: First, the road, which this path first walked in year one. In Luke's Gospel, robbers strip a traveler and leave him by the road. A priest comes by and passes on the other side.
A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, someone the listeners would have expected to keep his distance, stops, binds the wounds, and pays for the man's care at an inn. Second, the mirror.
Francis says each of us can find ourselves in every character: sometimes the wounded man, sometimes the robbers, or the ones who pass by.

He asks how often people look away, busy, sure it's someone else's job, and he notices that the passersby were religious men. Faith alone, in this story, doesn't make anyone stop. Third, the question flipped.

teach.h: NOT WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR, BUT BECOME ONE.
teach.b: A lawyer had asked Jesus, who is my neighbor? Jesus answers with the story, then turns the question around, in the Douay-Rheims: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?"
The question isn't who counts as my neighbor. It's whether I'll become one. Fourth, the title.
Jesus tells his disciples, "all you are brethren." Francis widens that circle to every person, across borders and parties and faiths.
In the letter he writes of his conversations with a Muslim leader, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, and of their shared call to fraternity.

teach.h: GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.
teach.b: And the story ends with an instruction anyone can carry: "Go, and do thou in like manner." This week's thread, from the gospel of life to this road: no one is a stranger to be passed by.

how: Catholic parishes and schools study Fratelli Tutti, often alongside the parable of the good Samaritan, and some use it in interfaith gatherings and in ministries that visit people on the margins.

games.q: a man lies beaten on the road to Jericho. a priest and a Levite have passed by. what does the Samaritan do?
o: pass by on the other side.
stop, bind his wounds, and pay for his care.
call out that help will come later.
games.why: the Samaritan stops, binds the wounds and pays at the inn. Jesus ends: "Go, and do thou in like manner."

practice: Picture a place you pass every day, a corner, a hallway, a parking lot, a group chat, and the person usually there on the edge whom you walk past, maybe not from unkindness, just from hurry.
Imagine slowing down instead: a greeting, a question, five minutes. If you pray, ask God for the Samaritan's eyes; if you don't, simply hold the picture of yourself stopping.

wordCard.voice: Fratelli Tutti. All brothers: Francis's letter on fraternity, built around the good Samaritan. Today's word, and the end of this week.

orig.note: Italian, not Latin: all brothers, the words Francis of Assisi used to address his brothers and sisters.

carryVoice: Your line: all brothers and sisters. The road to Jericho runs past every door. That's the week.
